intro: Higashiomi maps three trees. Two are hananoki, Acer pycnanthum, standing 600 metres apart in neighbouring hamlets: the westernmost wild specimens of this rare maple known anywhere in Japan, both National Natural Monuments since March 1921, both having survived storms that took off their main trunks. The third, a kilometre from the pair, is a temple's stand-in for the Buddha's own bodhi tree, a linden that grew back from its own scorched stump after a 1573 fire. None of the three sit within sight of one another; Higashiomi's research is not finished.
meta_description: Three trees in Higashiomi, Japan: the westernmost wild hananoki maples known anywhere, and a temple linden that regrew after a 16th century fire.
question_meta: Higashiomi's oldest mapped tree is a temple linden put at a thousand years by tradition, regrown after a 1573 fire, ahead of two rare wild maples nearby.
question_answer: Higashiomi's oldest mapped tree is the Sennen Bodaiju at Hyakusai-ji temple, a Miquel's linden traditionally reckoned at about a thousand years old, a figure that comes from temple tradition rather than a documented planting date. Its trunk was scorched when Oda Nobunaga's forces burned the temple to the ground in 1573, and it resprouted from its own base. About a kilometre away stand Higashiomi's two hananoki maples, the westernmost known wild specimens of the species, both designated National Natural Monuments on the same day, 3 March 1921: Minamihanazawa's tree is estimated at over 250 years and possibly over 450, Kitahanazawa's at over 300.
question_context: The thousand-year figure for the Hyakusai-ji linden is a round number Japanese temples have long given their oldest trees, not a ring count, and the temple's own material simply repeats it. What is documented is the fire: Oda Nobunaga burned Hyakusai-ji to the ground in 1573, scorching the linden without reaching its roots, so it grew back around its own dead wood. It stands in place of a true bodhi tree, Ficus religiosa, which cannot survive a Japanese winter, and carries no monument designation of its own. The hananoki pair, a kilometre away, do carry an individual designation, since 3 March 1921. Hananoki grows wild in only a handful of wet valleys in central Japan, and these two are its westernmost known specimens. Minamihanazawa's tree, 5.2 metres round, lost its main trunk to lightning-related rot in 2010. Kitahanazawa's, smaller at 2.8 metres round, has lost two trunks to storms and now grows as six limbs from one base. Both flower in late March and early April, and a ten-minute bus from Yokaichi Station reaches both. The temple linden is a separate trip, with its own admission and hours.

faq.a: Acer pycnanthum, a maple that grows wild in only a few wet valleys in central Japan. Two of Higashiomi's three trees are its westernmost known wild specimens.

faq.q: Which of the three trees is oldest?
faq.a: By tradition, the Hyakusai-ji temple linden, put at about a thousand years, though that figure is temple lore rather than a measurement. Of the two hananoki, Minamihanazawa is estimated slightly older than Kitahanazawa, but neither carries a hard date.

faq.q: Can all three trees be visited in one trip?
faq.a: The two hananoki stand about 600 metres apart, both reachable by the same ten-minute bus from Yokaichi Station. The temple linden is about a kilometre further on and is worth treating as a separate stop, since Hyakusai-ji charges admission (600 yen) and keeps its own hours.

faq.q: When is the best time to see them?
faq.a: Late March into early April for the hananoki, when the red flowers open on bare wood before either maple comes into leaf. The temple linden has no comparable recorded peak.

trees.name: Minamihanazawa no Hananoki

location.address: Hachiman Shrine grounds, Minamihanazawa-cho 546, Higashiomi City, Shiga Prefecture, Japan

trees.access: Free, in the grounds of Hachiman Shrine (the tree is the shrine's sacred tree); reachable by a ~10 minute bus from Yokaichi Station (Omi Railway) or ~10 minutes by car from Meishin Expressway's Yokaichi IC (per the official Biwako Visitors tourism site, biwako-visitors.jp)
trees.transport: ~10 min bus from Yokaichi Station (Omi Railway); pairs with its companion tree 600m north at Kitahanazawa for one short walk.
trees.story:
In August 2010 the main trunk of this maple rotted through from the inside, after lightning, and came down. The tree is still here.

It is a hananoki, Acer pycnanthum, a maple that grows wild in only a handful of wet valleys in central Japan. This one and its companion 600 metres north are the westernmost naturally occurring specimens known, and both were made National Natural Monuments on the same day in March 1921. It is the sacred tree of Hachiman Shrine at Minamihanazawa, 5.2 metres round at chest height and 21 metres tall.

Hananoki means flower tree, and the name is earned in early spring, when dense red flowers crowd the bare twigs before a single leaf opens.

Two things are disputed and worth saying plainly. Japanese Wikipedia puts the tree at over 250 years, a local account at over 450, and nobody has settled it. And the sources part company on what the 2010 collapse actually left: Wikipedia says the tree survived and pushed out new growth from the branches it still had, while a later account describes what remains as preserved rather than living. A photograph taken at these coordinates in September 2019 shows a tree standing, which is the reading this page follows. If you have been past more recently, tell us what you found.

best_time.label: late March and early April, when the red flowers crowd the bare twigs before the leaves

trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-09: checked after a photo pass read the Commons files as a dead trunk. The tree is ALIVE. ja.wikipedia's article on the monument says of the 2010 collapse 「ただし枯死だけはまぬがれ」, it escaped dying outright, and that new shoots grew from the surviving western limb and it flowered abundantly the following spring. The preserved trunk in the wooden shelter on Commons is the fallen main stem, kept as a display; the living tree is the regrowth. Female saplings were brought from Gifu in the 2000s as supplementary planting and are separate trees, which is what Commons files titled 'successor trees' show.

trees.name: Kitahanazawa no Hananoki

location.address: Kitahanazawa hamlet, Higashiomi City, Shiga Prefecture, Japan, approximately 600m north of Minamihanazawa no Hananoki

trees.access: Free; same tourism entry as Minamihanazawa (biwako-visitors.jp): ~10 min bus from Yokaichi Station (Omi Railway) to 'Kitahanazawa', or ~10 min by car from Meishin Expressway's Yokaichi IC
trees.transport: ~10 min bus from Yokaichi Station; 600m from its Minamihanazawa companion tree, both would form one short walk if paired together
trees.story:
This maple has lost two trunks to storms and is standing on what was left over. It forked near the base originally. One limb broke in a storm in 1866, the other went down in Typhoon Jane in 1950, and the tree today divides into six limbs about three metres up.

It is a hananoki, Acer pycnanthum, and together with its companion 600 metres south at Minamihanazawa it is one of the two westernmost naturally occurring specimens known in Japan. The pair were designated National Natural Monuments together on 3 March 1921, in the same order, and they still read as a pair: a ten minute bus from Yokaichi Station reaches both, and the walk between them is about ten minutes more.

The numbers: 4.9 metres round at the base, 2.8 at chest height, 17.27 metres tall. Japanese Wikipedia estimates it at over 300 years, which would have it already grown when the first of those two storms took a trunk off it.

Hananoki means flower tree. In early spring the red flowers open on bare wood, before any leaf, and the crown turns red before it turns green. The rest of the year it looks like an ordinary maple standing above a small Shiga hamlet, which is a fair share of the appeal: this is a nationally protected tree with no gate, no ticket and usually nobody else there.

best_time.label: late March and early April, when the red flowers open on bare wood before any leaf

trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-09: checked alongside hga_001. The designated tree is alive and standing. ja.wikipedia records it as hollow through most of the trunk with poor vigour 「幹の内部はほとんどが空洞で樹勢はあまり良い状態ではない」, about half its former size, 6 limbs from 3 m up. Three hananoki were planted as successor trees in Hananoki Park in 2002; those are NOT this tree, and Commons files titled 'successor trees of' must never be attached to it.

trees.name: The Sennen Bodaiju of Hyakusai-ji

location.address: Hyakusai-ji Temple, Hyakusaiji-cho, Higashiomi City, Shiga Prefecture, in the former front garden of the old main hall

trees.access: Paid entry to Hyakusai-ji, part of the Koto Sanzan (three temples of eastern Lake Biwa): 600 yen adults, open 8:30-17:00.
trees.transport: Bus from Yokaichi Station, about 30 minutes.
trees.story:
Oda Nobunaga burned Hyakusai-ji to the ground on 7 April 1573, and the tree in the front garden grew back out of its own scorched trunk. The fire charred the bark and never reached the roots, so fresh growth rose around the burn. What stands in the old main hall's garden today is regrowth from the base of the tree Nobunaga's men torched. The temple still tells that story, and still offers the tree as a charm against misfortune.

Its name is Sennen Bodaiju, the thousand-year bodhi tree, and it is a substitute. The bodhi tree of Buddhism is Ficus religiosa, a fig that will not survive a Japanese winter, so temples here plant Tilia miqueliana instead and give it the same name and the same spot in the garden. This one measures about five metres round, with a trunk roughly 1.6 metres across. The thousand years in the name is a traditional round figure rather than a date anyone recorded, so read it as many centuries and not as a measurement. If somebody has properly aged it, tell us.

Hyakusai-ji is one of the Koto Sanzan, the three old temples on the eastern flank of Lake Biwa. Entry costs 600 yen and the gates are open from 8:30 to 17:00, which buys the halls and the garden as well as the tree.
